target_customer: Bay Area renters and buyers wanting cheap small homes, sold or rented as shipping container units
problem: Rents in San Francisco rose fast, and the founders wanted portable, affordable housing built from shipping containers.
business_model: Build and sell or rent container homes and units on rented land

founders.name: Luke Iseman
founders.background_notes: Wrote the closing post (worked on boxouse about 2.5 years). A search result says he was Director of Hardware at Y Combinator 2015 to 2016, from a Wellfound profile I did not open, so it is not recorded as a prior employer.

founders.name: Heather
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder on the YC page and in the closing post, which says she worked on it just over a year. Surname not confirmed by an opened source.

exit.reason: The founders say the sales model did not work financially and permitting cost and time made fully legal installations too expensive

technical_complexity.rationale: Retrofitting used containers with insulation, power and plumbing is construction work using standard methods; the hard part was permits, not engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Plans were later released openly under CC BY-SA 4.0 and container conversion was widely copied; no structural moat.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent mattered. Local code enforcement in Oakland and San Francisco was the main opponent.

market_need_then: San Francisco rents were surging; the founders started in 2013 on a vacant lot. Press from 2015 to 2017 (SF Public Press, KALW, Bloomberg) covered demand and the code conflicts.

branding.domain_note: boxouse.com, an exact .com for the coined spelling; it now holds the closing announcement

identity.visual_style: Portable, beautiful smart homes with a luxury edition with wheels and solar power per the YC page
identity.voice_and_tone: Candid, personal founder voice in the closing post with itemized thanks and finances

branding.brand_signature: Open sourced plans and the Pod Mahal Burning Man build (2018)
branding.community_and_virality: Started as a community of friends on a vacant lot; heavy local and national press (CBS, KQED, Business Insider, Bloomberg) and open source plans praised on Permies forum

brand_strength.rationale: Distinctive coined name and strong press and community attention relative to its size, though the spelling confuses with 'box house' and the brand did not carry the business.

pivots.to: Regenerative farming and robotics (founders' stated next work, not a company pivot)
pivots.why: Sales model unprofitable and permitting too costly

outcome_analysis: Boxouse built about 11 container homes over roughly 2.5 years and raised about $280K including Y Combinator, with revenue near $414K against expenses near $489K for a net loss of about $75K, per the founders' closing post. They say the sales model did not work financially and that permitting cost and time made legal installations too expensive, and press from 2015 to 2016 documented code enforcement pushing the Oakland cluster to move. The founders covered losses except for investors and open sourced the plans under CC BY-SA 4.0.
notes: Company post gives total raised of about $280K including Y Combinator support, but only a $120K Y Combinator figure from CB Insights (single database, undated) is recorded as a round, so about $160K is unattributed. Closing post date is not given on the page. Competitors: Honomobo with Soup (Menlo Park, January 2017) surfaced in one search summary without a citable URL, so the list is empty. Bloomberg article (2017-03-16) could not be fetched due to a bot block; its details come from a search summary (deluxe edition $49,000, containers bought for about $2,000). Founded 2013 per the YC description. Founder education not found in opened sources.
